definition.text: Arthur Cecil Pigou (1877–1959) was an English economist, best known for the idea of taxing activities that cause negative externalities.

facts.text: In The Economics of Welfare (1920) he introduced the externality concept and the idea that a tax could correct externality problems, now called a Pigouvian tax.
He argued that harmful side effects should be offset by a tax and beneficial ones by a subsidy.
He studied under Alfred Marshall and succeeded him as Professor of Political Economy at Cambridge in 1908.
In the early 1960s Ronald Coase criticised his analysis, arguing that taxes and subsidies are unnecessary if the parties can bargain.
The externality concept remains central to welfare economics and especially to environmental economics.
The Pigou Club, named after him, groups modern economists who back a carbon tax against climate change.

definition.text: Elinor Ostrom (1933–2012) was an American political scientist and political economist who showed how communities can manage shared resources themselves.

facts.text: Against the predictions of the tragedy of the commons, her field studies showed users of pastures, fisheries and forests making their own rules to manage them sustainably.
In Governing the Commons (1990) she summarized eight design principles shared by long-lasting common-pool resource institutions.
She favoured a polycentric approach, with key management decisions made as close as possible to the places and people involved, rather than a single global authority.
With co-researchers she built the Social-Ecological Systems (SES) framework for studying common-pool resources and self-governance.
In 2009 she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, shared with Oliver E. Williamson.
The Nobel citation said her work showed common resources can be managed successfully without government regulation or privatization.
"Ostrom's law" sums up her challenge to theory: a resource arrangement that works in practice can work in theory.

definition.text: Herman Daly (1938–2022) was an American ecological economist, best known as a senior economist at the World Bank and for the idea of a steady-state economy.

facts.text: As Senior Economist in the World Bank's Environment Department he helped draft policy guidelines on sustainable development.
He co-founded the journal Ecological Economics and served as an associate editor.
His 1973 anthology Toward a Steady-State Economy gathered writers such as Georgescu-Roegen, Boulding and Hardin, and was revised in 1980 and 1993.
In 1989 he and John B. Cobb proposed the Index of Sustainable Economic Welfare as a better measure of progress than GDP.
He is widely credited with originating the idea of uneconomic growth, though some credit Marilyn Waring.
He drew on his professor Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen's view linking the economy to the entropy law.
In 1996 he received the Right Livelihood Award for defining a path of ecological economics joining ethics, quality of life, environment and community.

definition.text: John V. Krutilla (1922–2003) was an American environmental economist who invented the concept of existence value, the economic value of undisturbed wilderness.

facts.text: He introduced existence value, the value of an amenity such as wilderness or a species simply existing, in his essay "Conservation Reconsidered".
He has been described as creating or stimulating most of the agenda of modern environmental economics.
He worked at Resources for the Future until retiring in 1988, and shared the first Volvo Environment Prize with Allen V. Kneese in 1990.

definition.text: Kate Raworth (born 1970) is an English economist known for doughnut economics, a model balancing essential human needs against planetary boundaries.

facts.text: She first set out the doughnut idea in a 2012 paper and expanded it in her 2017 book Doughnut Economics.
She criticises the principle of unlimited growth as destroying planetary resources while serving human needs poorly.
Her model aims to give everyone basic needs such as food and education without limiting future generations' opportunities.
She worked on the UN Human Development Report and spent over a decade as a senior researcher at Oxfam.

definition.text: Kenneth Boulding (1910–1993) was an English-born American economist, educator, peace activist and interdisciplinary thinker.

facts.text: His 1966 essay "The Economics of the Coming Spaceship Earth" argued that the economy must fit itself to an ecological system with limited resources.
He suggested treating Earth's ecosystem as a stock of assets.
He stressed that economic behaviour is embedded in a larger interconnected system and promoted an evolutionary rather than equilibrium approach to economics.

title: Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen

definition.text: Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen (1906–1994) was a Romanian mathematician, statistician and economist whose work on entropy and natural resources helped found ecological economics.

facts.text: His 1971 book The Entropy Law and the Economic Process argued that all natural resources are irreversibly degraded when used in economic activity.
He described the economy as turning valuable low-entropy resources into worthless high-entropy waste and pollution, which is why resources are scarce.
He argued Earth's carrying capacity will shrink as its finite mineral stock is used up, leading the world economy towards eventual collapse.
By bringing resource flows into economic models, his work was decisive in establishing ecological economics as a separate sub-discipline in the 1980s.
He taught Herman Daly, but later criticised his student's steady-state economy in several articles.
The degrowth movement of the early 2000s treats him as its main intellectual influence.
Mistakes from his incomplete grasp of thermodynamics have caused controversy among physicists and ecological economists.

contested_note: His application of thermodynamics to economics contains mistakes that physicists and ecological economists have argued over.

title: Nicholas Stern
article: Nicholas Stern, Baron Stern of Brentford

definition.text: Nicholas Stern (born 1946) is a British economist, banker and academic who led the Stern Review on the economics of climate change.

facts.text: The Stern Review, produced by his team at HM Treasury, was released in October 2006.
The Review described climate change as an externality, and Stern later called it the greatest market failure the world has seen.
It recommended regulation, carbon taxes, carbon trading, pollution permits and property rights, and urged immediate emission cuts at a significant but manageable cost.
Economists reacted in mixed ways; some called the Review deeply flawed, while others found its conclusions reasonable even if its method was wrong.
He chairs the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the London School of Economics.

contested_note: Economists disagreed over the Stern Review, some calling it deeply flawed and others defending its conclusions.

definition.text: Sir Partha Dasgupta (born 1942) is an Indian-British economist at the University of Cambridge whose long-standing interest is ecological economics.

facts.text: With Karl-Göran Mäler he developed 'inclusive wealth' as a measure of human well-being.
His 1982 monograph The Control of Resources set a research agenda linking population, consumption and the natural environment.
He led The Economics of Biodiversity: The Dasgupta Review, commissioned by the UK government and published in February 2021.
The Review aimed at a measure of natural capital usable in judging investment projects and the sustainability of economic programmes.
The Review rebuilds growth, development and poverty economics on the view that the human economy is embedded in Nature, not external to it.
He helped set up the journal Environment and Development Economics in 1996.

title: Pavan Sukhdev

definition.text: Pavan Sukhdev (born 1960) is an Indian environmental economist working on the green economy, biodiversity, natural capital and sustainable finance.

facts.text: He was Study Leader of TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity), a G8+5 study hosted by UNEP.
TEEB's 2008 Interim Report showed the economic significance of losing nature's services and linked it to ethics, equity and poverty reduction.
He headed UNEP's Green Economy Initiative, which argued that greening economies drives wealth, jobs and poverty reduction rather than burdening growth.
A banker by background, he spent 14 years at Deutsche Bank and was president of WWF International from 2017 to 2021.

prerequisites: The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity

definition.text: Robert Costanza (born 1950) is an American/Australian ecological economist at University College London's Institute for Global Prosperity.

facts.text: He co-founded the International Society for Ecological Economics, was its first president, and was founding chief editor of its journal Ecological Economics from 1989 to 2002.
In 1997 he led an attempted valuation of the global ecosystem, published in Nature.
The study put the value of ecosystem services at $33 trillion a year, within a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion, when global GDP was $27 trillion.
Half of that value came from nutrient cycling.
His work lumped ecosystem goods and services together as ecosystem services, unlike Gretchen Daily's original definition.
He studied under H.T. Odum and directed the Gund Institute for Ecological Economics at the University of Vermont.

definition.text: Ronald Coase (1910–2013) was a British economist whose work on transaction costs and property rights reshaped how economists think about externalities.

facts.text: His 1960 paper "The Problem of Social Cost" argued that it is unclear where the blame for an externality lies.
His example was a rancher whose cattle stray onto a neighbour's crops: restraining the cattle harms the rancher just as unrestrained cattle harm the farmer.
He argued that without transaction costs, the initial assignment of property rights does not affect whether the efficient outcome is reached.
The Coase theorem says that with tradeable externalities and low enough transaction costs, bargaining reaches an efficient outcome whatever the starting allocation of property.
In practice, obstacles to bargaining or poorly defined property rights can block Coasean bargaining.
His analysis challenged Pigou's: he argued taxes and subsidies are unnecessary if the parties can bargain.
His 1937 essay "The Nature of the Firm" explained firms as a way of avoiding the transaction costs of using the market.

title: William Nordhaus

definition.text: William Nordhaus (1941–2026) was an American economist at Yale, best known for economic modelling of climate change.

facts.text: He shared the 2018 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Paul Romer, for integrating climate change into long-run macroeconomic analysis.
He developed the DICE and RICE integrated assessment models linking economics, energy use and climate change.
His model is used to examine the effects of climate policies such as carbon taxes.
He was an early advocate of carbon taxes or other ways of pricing carbon dioxide emissions.
In 1972, with James Tobin, he introduced the Measure of Economic Welfare as a first attempt at environmental accounting.
In 2007 he criticised the Stern Review for using a low discount rate.
Critics fault DICE's discounting, its damage function and its handling of low-probability, high-consequence 'fat tail' outcomes, and some objected to his low carbon tax levels.

contested_note: Economists and climate scientists dispute his model's discounting, damage function and low recommended carbon taxes.

definition.text: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948) was an American forester, ecologist, writer and conservationist, known for his land ethic.

facts.text: His land ethic widens the idea of community to include soils, waters, plants and animals, together called the land.
He described conservation as a state of harmony between people and land, in his posthumous 1949 book A Sand County Almanac.
His 1933 book Game Management helped found wildlife management as a science and was its leading textbook for over 40 years.
In 1921 he argued for preserving roadless wilderness in national forests, proposing the Gila headwaters as a prime case.

title: Garrett Hardin

definition.text: Garrett Hardin (1915–2003) was an American ecologist and microbiologist, best known for his 1968 paper "The Tragedy of the Commons".

facts.text: His 1968 Science paper drew attention to the damage that innocent individual actions can do to the environment.
The essay drew on an 1833 pamphlet by William Forster Lloyd about herders overgrazing a shared parcel of land.
He applied the model to population growth, natural resource use and the welfare state, writing that freedom in a commons brings ruin to all.
Critics said he ignored the demographic transition and confused common property with open-access resources, and Elinor Ostrom's work contradicted his pessimism.
His First Law of Human Ecology holds that we can never do just one thing, since any intrusion into nature has many unpredictable effects.
His hardline positions on immigration, race and eugenics have led several sources to label him a white nationalist.

contested_note: His tragedy-of-the-commons argument is disputed by critics and contradicted by Ostrom's field studies of successful commons.

definition.text: Gretchen Daily (born 1964) is an American environmental scientist and tropical ecologist who advanced the science of ecosystem services and ways to value nature in decisions.

facts.text: She edited Nature's Services: Societal Dependence on Natural Ecosystems (1997), a foundational framework for understanding nature's benefits to people.
Nature's Services served as a model for ecosystem regulation in several regions and was a catalyst for the UN's Millennium Ecosystem Assessment.
Her original definition kept ecosystem goods and ecosystem services apart, a distinction later work lumped together.
In 2005 she co-founded the Natural Capital Project with The Nature Conservancy and World Wildlife Fund to bring nature's values into decision-making.
The Project's open-source software InVEST is used in 185 countries to show nature's values in specific decisions.
Her 2002 book with Katherine Ellison, The New Economy of Nature, gives cases where companies or governments profited from conservation.

definition.text: Allen V. Kneese (1930–2001) was an American economist and a pioneer of environmental economics.

facts.text: His research built pollution into economic models and studied economic incentives for environmental improvement.
He was the first president of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and a founding editor of the Journal of Environmental Economics and Management.
He worked at Resources for the Future from 1961, and shared the first Volvo Environment Prize with John V. Krutilla in 1990.

definition.text: AnnMari Jansson (1934–2007) was a Swedish systems ecologist who helped pioneer research joining ecology and economics.

facts.text: In 1982, with economist Karl-Göran Mäler, she gathered ecologists and economists at a Saltsjöbaden symposium on integrating ecology and economy.
She helped found the International Society for Ecological Economics in 1988 and edited its journal Ecological Economics from 1989.
Her ecological work drew on the models of Howard T. Odum.

definition.text: C. S. 'Buzz' Holling (1930–2019) was a Canadian ecologist and one of the conceptual founders of ecological economics.

facts.text: He introduced ideas including resilience, adaptive management, the adaptive cycle and panarchy.
His 1973 paper on the resilience of ecological systems had a large impact across natural and social sciences.
In his usage, resilience is an ecosystem's resistance to shifting into another state.
He was among the first ecologists to recognise the importance of nonlinear dynamics.
He founded the Resilience Alliance and the journal Conservation Ecology, now Ecology and Society.

definition.text: David Pearce (1941–2005) was a British pioneer of environmental economics and professor at University College London.

facts.text: He set out techniques for valuing nature, arguing that the environment is under-priced and that the benefits of environmental services can be calculated.
His early work on cost-benefit analysis, pollution and resource depletion came before these ideas reached mainstream economics and policy.
He advised UK ministers and was a convening lead author for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.
He criticised the assumptions behind discounting future goods.

definition.text: Dennis Meadows (born 1942) is an American systems scientist best known as a co-author of The Limits to Growth.

facts.text: From 1970 to 1972 at MIT he directed the Club of Rome project that built the world computer model behind The Limits to Growth.
The 1972 book used the World3 model to explore how exponential growth interacts with finite resources, rather than to make specific predictions.
By the 2004 30-Year Update the message had shifted from slowing growth to managing an orderly reduction of activity back below the Earth's limits.
He received the Japan Prize in 2009 for work towards a sustainable society in harmony with nature.

definition.text: Donella Meadows (1941–2001) was an American environmental scientist and writer, best known as lead author of The Limits to Growth and Thinking in Systems.

facts.text: In 1972 she was on the MIT team that built the World3 global computer model for the Club of Rome, the basis of The Limits to Growth.
The book studied long-term global trends in population, economics and the environment and began a still-running debate about the limits of Earth's capacity to support economic expansion.
Her 1999 essay Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System describes the most and least effective kinds of intervention in any system.
With Dennis Meadows she created the Balaton Group in 1982, a network of researchers on resource use, conservation, systems modelling and sustainability.
She trained under Jay Forrester's system dynamics group at MIT and later taught at Dartmouth College for 29 years.

definition.text: E. F. Schumacher (1911–1977) was a German-born British economist best known for proposing human-scale, decentralised and appropriate technologies.

facts.text: He first coined the term 'natural capital', in his 1973 book Small Is Beautiful.
Small Is Beautiful argues that production cannot be called solved if it recklessly erodes finite natural capital and robs future generations of its benefits.
He coined 'Buddhist economics' in 1955 while working as an economic consultant in Burma, holding that people need good work to develop properly.
He pioneered appropriate technology, meaning user-friendly, ecologically suitable technology scaled to the community, and founded the Intermediate Technology Development Group in 1966.
As chief economic adviser to the National Coal Board from 1950 to 1970 he saw oil as a finite resource and feared its depletion.
Key ideas of ecological economics appear in his writings and in Kenneth Boulding's.

definition.text: Gifford Pinchot (1865–1946) was an American forester and politician, a key figure in the history of conservation and natural resource management in the United States.

facts.text: He promoted scientific forestry and the controlled, profitable use of forests and other natural resources for the greatest benefit to people.
In 1905 he and Theodore Roosevelt persuaded Congress to create the United States Forest Service, and he became its first chief.
He advocated the wise use of natural resources, framing conservation as a way to secure long-term benefits for society.
Joan Martinez Alier names him one of the leading proponents of the 'gospel of eco-efficiency'.

definition.text: Harold Hotelling (1895–1973) was an American mathematical statistician and economic theorist, known for Hotelling's law, Hotelling's lemma and Hotelling's rule.

facts.text: His 1931 analysis of non-renewable resource management in the Journal of Political Economy produced Hotelling's rule.
Hotelling's rule, a price path for exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels, is one of the best-known early works on the economics of exhaustible resources.
He pioneered the study of non-convexities, which are linked to market failures and arise with environmental goods and other externalities.
He became an early advocate of congestion pricing, a toll meant to change behaviour rather than recoup investment costs.
His 1929 article founded spatial economics, treating space as a field where competitors jostle to be nearest their customers.
He argued in 1938 that selling at marginal cost is a condition of maximum general welfare.

title: Howard T. Odum

definition.text: Howard T. Odum (1924–2002) was an American ecologist known for pioneering ecosystem ecology and for linking ecological energy flows to economics.

facts.text: He modelled the energy flow pathways of ecosystems with analogue electrical circuits, one of the earliest instances of systems ecology.
While directing the University of Texas Marine Institute (1956–1963) he funded research using conventional economics to put dollar values on ecological resources.
He coined the term ecological engineering in 1962.
In the 1990s he and David Scienceman developed emergy, a measure of energy used in the past; the idea remains controversial and little recognised.
He took part in the 1982 meeting in Sweden that helped launch ecological economics, alongside Robert Costanza and Herman Daly.

contested_note: His concept of emergy is disputed and has been demonstrated in only a few experiments.

definition.text: Joan Martinez Alier (born 1939) is a Spanish economist whose work in ecological economics and political ecology is summed up in the idea of the environmentalism of the poor.

facts.text: He argues, against neoclassical economists, that the economy is not circular but entropic: energy is not recycled and materials only partly so.
With Martin O'Connor he introduced ecological distribution conflicts in 1995 as a concept for documenting and analysing environmental conflicts.
He describes the environmentalism of the poor as the struggles poor people wage when ecological distribution conflicts threaten them.
He is a founding member and past president of the International Society for Ecological Economics.
He won the 2023 Holberg Prize for research in ecological economics, political ecology and environmental justice.

definition.text: Karl William Kapp (1910–1976) was a German-American economist whose theory of social costs makes him a foundational thinker of social ecological economics.

facts.text: His theory of social costs addresses urgent socio-ecological problems and proposes preventive policies based on the precautionary principle.
He argued that 'externality' is a misnomer, and his theory offers the heterodox alternative to the neoclassical definition of social cost.
His 1950 work is counted among the European predecessors of ecological economics.

definition.text: Karl-Göran Mäler (1939–2020) was a Swedish economist known for his work in economics and ecological economics.

facts.text: In 1992 he and Partha Dasgupta founded the Beijer Institute of Ecological Economics, which he directed until 2006.
He and Dasgupta shared the Volvo Environment Prize in 2002.
He was a professor at the Stockholm School of Economics from 1975 to 2002.

definition.text: Mathis Wackernagel is a Swiss-born sustainability advocate who co-created the ecological footprint and heads the Global Footprint Network.

facts.text: The ecological footprint concept and calculation method was his PhD work with supervisor William Rees at the University of British Columbia, from 1990 to 1994.
Footprint and biocapacity accounts compare human demand on nature with what nature can supply, and Global Footprint Network has developed them further since 2003.
He holds that climate change, biodiversity loss and food shortage are symptoms of one theme: humanity's use of resources has grown large compared with what Earth can renew.
With Rees he proposed that cost savings from efficiency gains be taxed away so they cannot cause a rebound in use.

definition.text: Milner Baily Schaefer (1912–1970) was an American fisheries scientist notable for his work on the population dynamics of fisheries.

facts.text: At the Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission he published a fishery equilibrium model based on the Verhulst growth model, with a catch equation known as the Schaefer short-term catch equation.
He extended the model to an unregulated fishery where effort rises until no profit is left, the equilibrium H. Scott Gordon called bionomic equilibrium.
Together, Schaefer's and Gordon's work, now the Gordon–Schaefer model, laid the basis for quantitative fisheries economics.

title: Rachel Carson

definition.text: Rachel Carson (1907–1964) was an American marine biologist, writer and conservationist whose book Silent Spring (1962) is credited with advancing the global environmental movement.

facts.text: Silent Spring described the harmful effects of pesticides on the environment and helped focus opposition to DDT.
She argued pesticides are better called biocides because their effects rarely stay limited to the target pests.
One scholar wrote that after Silent Spring no one could easily sell pollution as the necessary underside of progress.

notes: Shaped environmentalism rather than environmental, ecological or resource economics; kept only so the coordinator can decide.

definition.text: Richard B. Norgaard (born 1943) is an American professor emeritus of ecological economics at the University of California, Berkeley, considered one of the field's founders.

facts.text: His research treats development as a process of coevolution between social and environmental systems.
A 1975 paper showed farmers who hired independent pest-control experts earned more and used half as much pesticide as those advised by agribusiness.
He was president of the International Society for Ecological Economics from 1998 to 2001.
In Development Betrayed he argues traditional economics has hijacked the language of development.

definition.text: Robert Ayres (1932–2023) was an American-born physicist and economist who applied the laws of thermodynamics to economics and originated the idea of industrial metabolism.

facts.text: He pioneered the field sometimes called industrial metabolism or industrial ecology, the study of material flows and transformations.
He argued that the first law of thermodynamics makes 'consumption' misleading, because transforming materials unavoidably creates large amounts of waste, some of it toxic.
He criticised growth models whose production functions leave out energy, as if output came from labour and capital alone.
With Benjamin Warr he found growth accounting improves when the efficiency of energy conversion is included.
He is named among the figures of ecological economics.

definition.text: Serge Latouche (born 1940) is a French emeritus professor of economics and one of the best-known advocates of degrowth.

facts.text: He denounces economism, consumer society and the notion of sustainable development, and criticises economic efficiency and economic rationalism.
In Farewell to Growth he credited Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen as the main theoretical source of degrowth.
The same manifesto proposes 'ecomunicipalism' to start a virtuous cycle of quiet contraction of economic activity.

definition.text: Serhiy Podolynsky (1850–1891) was a Ukrainian socialist, physician and sociologist, an early pioneer of ecological economics.

facts.text: He tried to reconcile socialist thought with the second law of thermodynamics, drawing on Marx, Darwin and Sadi Carnot.
In 1880 he proposed a labour theory of value based on embodied energy; Marx and Engels read and critiqued it.
He held that human labour only changes natural objects, and that the resources available to people grow only through photosynthesis capturing the Sun's energy.

definition.text: William Baumol (1922–2017) was an American economist, among the world's most influential, whose work included environmental economics.

facts.text: He was instrumental in framing Pigou's work for modern economics in 1972.
His environmental economics research recognised the fundamental role of non-convexities in causing market failures.
He argued that the social cost of an externality is extraordinarily difficult, almost impossible, to measure, a key criticism of Pigouvian taxes.

title: William E. Rees

definition.text: William E. Rees is a Canadian human ecologist and ecological economist, best known for co-developing the ecological footprint with his graduate students.

facts.text: The ecological footprint estimates humanity's demand on nature through measurable flows of energy and materials to and from ecosystems.
He coined the term in 1990, replacing 'regional capsule' in a manuscript after a colleague's remark about his computer's small desk footprint.
He describes ecological overshoot as human demand on ecosystems exceeding Earth's capacity to regenerate and absorb wastes, beyond long-term global carrying capacity.
He criticises mainstream economics for treating nature as an externality and assuming perfect substitutability between manufactured and natural capital.
He argues growing economies remain dependent subsystems of the ecosphere, so growth is ultimately limited by its finite capacity.
Neoclassical economists and ecomodernists have pushed back against his theories.

contested_note: Neoclassical economists and ecomodernists dispute his view that growth is constrained by ecological limits.

definition.text: William Forster Lloyd (1794–1852) was an English writer on economics, best known for an 1833 lecture that first set out the tragedy of the commons.

facts.text: In Two Lectures on the Checks to Population (1833) he introduced the idea of a common being overused by those with rights to use it.
His example: herders each entitled to graze cows on shared land overuse it, to the detriment of all its users.
He reasoned that an extra animal on a common takes food shared among everyone's cattle, so only a small part of the cost falls on its owner.
H. Scott Gordon and later Garrett Hardin developed his idea; Hardin later said he should have called it the tragedy of the unmanaged commons.
He also gave an early statement of diminishing marginal utility, placing him among the proto-marginalists.

definition.text: William Stanley Jevons (1835–1882) was an English economist and logician, a leader of the marginal revolution and author of The Coal Question.

facts.text: In The Coal Question (1865) he drew attention to the gradual exhaustion of Britain's coal supplies.
He argued that improving energy efficiency lowers energy costs and so increases rather than decreases energy use, now called the Jevons paradox.
His Theory of Political Economy (1871) set out a theory of value based on marginal utility, developed independently of Menger and Walras.
Joan Martinez Alier traces the 'gospel of eco-efficiency' to the 19th-century writings of Malthus and Jevons.
His energy-depletion arguments have been revisited by writers on peak oil.

definition.text: Ecological Economics is a peer-reviewed journal published by Elsevier for the International Society for Ecological Economics, covering research on ecological economics.

facts.text: Robert Costanza founded it in 1989 as its first editor-in-chief.
It aims to integrate understanding of the interplay between 'nature's household' (ecosystems) and 'humanity's household' (the economy).
It publishes both neoclassical and heterodox work, which has sparked lively debate among the membership.

title: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management
article: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

definition.text: The Journal of Environmental Economics and Management is a peer-reviewed environmental economics journal published six times a year.

facts.text: It is generally regarded as the top journal in natural resource and environmental economics.
Ralph d'Arge and Allen V. Kneese were its founding editors, and it was the official journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists until 2014.

related: Review of Environmental Economics and Policy

title: Martin Faustmann

definition.text: A German forester regarded as the father of forest economics.

facts.text: His 1849 analysis of the optimal rotation problem, the Faustmann formula, is still widely used in natural resource valuation.
He became chief forester of Dudenhofen near Darmstadt after his 1848 examinations and stayed there until his death.

title: Martin Weitzman

definition.text: An American economist at Harvard whose research centred on environmental economics, especially climate change and catastrophes.

facts.text: He added the risk of dramatic climate change to cost-benefit analysis to argue for immediate action.
He argued that the economy-climate system may have fat tails that standard models handle poorly.
He showed when price controls beat quantity controls under uncertainty.
He co-wrote Climate Shock (2015) with Gernot Wagner.
